Note::strip¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signatures¶

Note Note::strip() const
Note Note::strip(std::string_view chars) const

Trim Characters From Both Ends Of Every Cell¶

strip() returns a new Note, same shape as the input, with leading and trailing whitespace removed from each cell. strip(chars) instead removes any character that appears in the chars set. Use it to clean boundary noise before comparison, tokenization, measurement, or display — padded fields, wrapping markers (##title##), stray delimiters at the ends of a concatenation.

strip() — whitespace¶

The no-argument form removes the ASCII whitespace bytes space, \t, \n, \r, \f, \v from both ends. Whitespace inside the cell is left exactly as-is — strip() is a boundary trim, not a normalizer. Combine with replace or a tokenizer if interior spacing also needs work.

strip(chars) — a character set¶

chars is treated as a set of bytes: every position at either end whose byte is in the set is removed, and trimming stops at the first byte that is not. Order and repetition in chars do not matter. So strip("#") removes runs of # from the ends only ("##a#b##" → "a#b"), and strip("xy-") removes any mix of x, y, - from the ends ("xy-payload-yx" → "payload"). Because the set is byte-based, pass only ASCII characters in chars; a multi-byte character there would match its individual bytes.

A cell made entirely of strippable characters becomes empty. The operation is shape-preserving, cell-independent, and returns a fresh Note.

Example 1: Trim Whitespace¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"  Ada Lovelace  ", "\tGRACE HOPPER\t", "Linus"}).strip())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["Ada Lovelace", "GRACE HOPPER", "Linus"]

Example 2: Interior Whitespace Is Kept¶

const pluss::Note n = pluss::make_note({"a\tb  c"}).strip();
std::cout << n << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["a\tb  c"]

There is no leading or trailing whitespace, so the cell is unchanged; the tab and double space between the letters stay.

Example 3: Strip A Character Set¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"##alpha##", "#beta", "gamma##", "#a#b#"}).strip("#"))
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["alpha", "beta", "gamma", "a#b"]

Only the # runs at the ends go; the # between a and b stays.

Example 4: A Set Of Several Characters¶

pluss::note::print(std::cout,
                   pluss::make_note({"xy-payload-yx"}).strip("xy-"))
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["payload"]

Any mix of x, y, - is trimmed from both ends until a different byte is reached.

Example 5: Fully Strippable Cells Become Empty¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"   ", "###"}).strip().strip("#"))
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["", ""]

Example 6: Shape Is Preserved¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({{"  a  ", "  b  "}}).strip())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[1, 2], dim=2, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
[
  ["a", "b"]
]

See Also¶

  • Note::lower: case-fold; commonly chained with strip for full normalization.

  • Note::remove_all: delete a substring anywhere, not just at the boundaries.

  • pluss::coden::Note::lstrip / rstrip: trim one end only.
